title: World Court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, a first against any state
dek: The International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that Myanmar's 2017 military operations in Rakhine were genocide and ordered it to allow refugees to return safely and pay compensation. Bangladesh, which shelters over a million Rohingya, called it historic.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during the military's 2017 "clearance operations" in northern Rakhine State, the first time the United Nations' highest court has found a state responsible for genocide. The judges voted 9-6 on the central finding, in a case brought by The Gambia in 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The court ordered Myanmar to end continuing violations of the convention, to investigate and prosecute those suspected of genocide, to give guarantees that it will not happen again, to allow the safe, voluntary and dignified return of Rohingya refugees, and to pay compensation, the amount of which will be set later. The ruling is final and cannot be appealed. For Bangladesh, which shelters more than a million Rohingya in camps around Cox's Bazar, and for India, which borders Rakhine and has invested in a transport corridor through it, the judgment changes the terms of a crisis that has lasted nine years.

## What the court found

The court found that Myanmar's security forces and other state organs killed Rohingya, caused serious bodily or mental harm, and imposed measures intended to prevent births, and that the intent to destroy the group in substantial part was "the only reasonable inference" from the evidence, according to a summary by Human Rights Watch. Court President Yuji Iwasawa said the evidence showed security forces had killed some 10,000 Rohingya, according to reports. The court also found widespread sexual violence and extreme violence against children.

Beyond the central finding, the court held that Myanmar had failed in its duties to prevent and to punish genocide, including by individuals acting alongside the security forces, and to pass the laws the convention requires. It also found that Myanmar had breached the court's order of 23 January 2020 to preserve evidence. It did not find that Myanmar had directly and publicly incited genocide. Myanmar must report to the court on the steps it has taken within two years, according to reports.

The votes on the other findings were narrower or wider than on genocide itself: 11-4 on the failure to punish and 10-5 on the restitution measures, according to reports. The court's website could not be reached for this report, so these vote counts rest on reports.

## Background

In August 2017, after attacks on police posts by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, Myanmar's army launched operations across northern Rakhine. Reports of the number who fled to Bangladesh in the months that followed range from more than 700,000 to more than 800,000. Myanmar has always said its forces were responding to militant attacks and has denied genocidal intent.

The Gambia, acting with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, filed the case in November 2019, arguing that every state party to the Genocide Convention has an interest in seeing it upheld. The court ordered provisional measures to protect the Rohingya in January 2020, rejected Myanmar's objections to its jurisdiction in July 2022, and heard the merits with 11 other states intervening on questions of how the convention should be read.

Since then, the Myanmar military that carried out the 2017 operations seized power in a coup in February 2021. The commander who led the army at the time, Min Aung Hlaing, is now the country's president. The Arakan Army, an ethnic armed group that is fighting the military, now controls much of the land the Rohingya fled, according to reports. Bangladesh shelters about 1.2 million to 1.3 million Rohingya, according to reports and the UN refugee agency, where aid cuts have reduced food rations.

## What they are saying

- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the ruling a "demonstration of international justice" and urged Myanmar to comply, according to reports.
- UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the judgment "clearly concludes" that Myanmar is responsible for "one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind".
- The government of The Gambia welcomed it with "profound satisfaction", calling it "a historic day for international justice".
- Bangladesh's foreign ministry called it "a historic milestone in securing justice and accountability for the Rohingya", said Myanmar "is now legally bound to comply fully", and said repatriation "remains the only viable solution to the crisis". Shama Obaed Islam, a state minister for foreign affairs, said the ruling would strengthen pressure on Myanmar and the Arakan Army to allow returns, according to reports.
- British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Britain would expel Myanmar's defence attaché, had summoned its chargé d'affaires and would seek an urgent UN Security Council meeting, according to reports.
- A US official said Washington was "studying the decision to fully assess its implications", according to reports.
- Myanmar's opposition National Unity Government said it respected the court's authority. Myanmar's government had not publicly responded by Friday morning.

India's Ministry of External Affairs had not commented on the ruling by Friday morning. China's foreign ministry did not address it at its regular briefing on Thursday.

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

India shares a land border with Myanmar and is building the Kaladan multi-modal transit project, which runs from Kolkata by sea to Sittwe port in Rakhine and then by river and road to Mizoram, through territory now contested between the army and the Arakan Army. A ruling that obliges Myanmar to take the Rohingya back, with international pressure behind it, bears directly on the stability of that corridor.

India is a party to the Genocide Convention and hosts Rohingya refugees of its own, many of whom it treats as illegal immigrants. Any renewed violence in Rakhine, or a further exodus into Bangladesh, would add to pressure on a neighbour already in political turmoil, and on the India-Bangladesh border along West Bengal. Dhaka has asked partners, including China and Russia, which have close ties with Myanmar's military, to press for returns, according to reports.

## What happens next

The court has no way of enforcing its rulings. If Myanmar does not comply, The Gambia can ask the UN Security Council to act, a power the council has never used; China and Russia hold vetoes there. The General Assembly can pass resolutions calling for compliance. A separate phase will fix the amount and form of compensation. Lawyers expect the judgment, the court's first full ruling of genocide against a state, to be cited in other pending cases under the convention, including South Africa's case against Israel.
